### Key takeaways


A modern identity attack in manufacturing occurs when adversaries bypass legacy network perimeters by compromising workforce credentials, unmanaged machine identities, or third-party vendor logins to pivot from corporate IT networks into shop-floor operational technology. To protect production uptime and intellectual property, manufacturers must replace static logins with phishing-resistant MFA, automated machine identity governance, continuous session evaluation, and just-in-time vendor access.


As smart factories accelerate the convergence of enterprise information technology (IT) and shop-floor operational technology (OT), **attackers are actively exploiting the identity seams between corporate networks, connected machinery, and external supply chains** .


For manufacturing and plant operations leaders, the stakes have fundamentally shifted. Digital systems no longer merely support the business; they physically drive production lines, calibrate industrial robotics, and govern proprietary product blueprints. Traditional perimeter firewalls and legacy air-gapped assumptions can no longer protect distributed plants, third-party field engineers, and autonomous industrial AI agents.


## Why identity is the primary battlefield in industrial cybersecurity


For manufacturing and plant operations leaders, the business impact of identity compromise is severe and tangible:


- **Top target for extortion:**[Manufacturing faces more ransomware and extortion attacks](https://www.halcyon.ai/blog/manufacturing-is-the-most-targeted-sector-in-ransomware) than any other sector worldwide, as attackers weaponize plant downtime to demand record-breaking ransoms.
- **Catastrophic breach costs:** For industrial manufacturers, the[average cost of a data breach](https://www.ibm.com/downloads/documents/us-en/16dd90a741c46c2c) is now $5.5 million.
- **Theft of crown-jewel intellectual property:** Nation-state actors and corporate espionage rings routinely target product designs, CAD schematics, proprietary chemistry formulations, and digital twins.
- **Stringent compliance and supply chain mandates:** Regulations such as **NIST SP 800-82** , **IEC 62443** , **NIS2** , and **CMMC 2.0** increasingly mandate phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and strict access governance across both IT systems and critical OT conduits.


## The four-phase IT-to-OT identity attack chain


While industrial environments range from discrete assembly plants to continuous process refineries, examining four interconnected phases illustrates how modern identity attacks penetrate manufacturing environments—and where leaders can erect decisive defenses.


Download[The Anatomy of Modern Identity Attacks: Security Cheatsheet](https://www.okta.com/resources/ebooks/the-anatomy-of-modern-identity-attacks-cheatsheet/) for a practical framework for understanding modern identity threats—from credential theft and adversary-in-the-middle attacks to the emerging security challenges posed by AI agents.


### Phase 1: How attackers breach the corporate perimeter with phishing and AiTM


Modern attacks on manufacturers seldom begin with physical sabotage or obscure industrial exploits; they start with stolen or spoofed digital credentials. Adversaries leverage generative AI to craft highly convincing, hyper-targeted social engineering campaigns:


- **Procurement and supplier lures:** Phishing emails sent to supply chain coordinators, plant engineers, or logistics managers reference authentic supplier part numbers, vendor RFPs, or enterprise resource planning (ERP) migrations.
- **Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) harvesting:** Attackers deploy reverse-proxy infrastructure to intercept both credentials and one-time MFA codes in real time, bypassing legacy SMS and basic push authenticators.
- **IT support and help desk manipulation:** Attackers use AI-cloned voices or forged documentation to impersonate plant technicians, claiming that accounts are locked during high-pressure shift rotations to trick service desk staff into resetting passwords or enrolling unauthorized devices.


Once attackers establish initial corporate access—often through enterprise email or SaaS project management suites—they secure a silent foothold inside the manufacturer’s corporate perimeter.


### Phase 2: Why industrial AI agents and machine identities are high-risk targets


The rapid rise of Industry 4.0 has introduced a vast web of non-human identities across manufacturing ecosystems. Autonomous AI agents now oversee predictive maintenance algorithms, optimize material-handling robotics, and automate quality inspections. Meanwhile, thousands of industrial internet of things (IIoT) sensors, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) gateways, and manufacturing execution systems (MES) continuously exchange data through machine-to-machine (M2M) APIs.


However, governance for non-human identities often lags far behind[workforce identity and access management](https://www.okta.com/products/workforce-identity/) :


- **Over-privileged service accounts:** Engineering tools and industrial telemetry pipelines frequently rely on static, shared service credentials with excessive read/write privileges spanning corporate databases and plant-floor control layers.
- **Compromised API tokens:** Long-lived access tokens embedded in development repositories or in unmanaged edge computing nodes provide attackers with unmonitored backdoors into industrial systems.
- **Agentic workflow manipulation:** As autonomous AI agents gain execution privileges to adjust machine tolerances or schedule maintenance batches, prompt injection and compromised orchestration pipelines introduce physical risks to equipment integrity and product specifications.


At machine speed, an unmanaged API token or agent credential transforms a corporate network intrusion into a direct threat to physical operations.


Read our whitepaper,[How Manufacturers Can Reap the Rewards of Digital Transformation](https://www.okta.com/resources/whitepapers/how-manufacturers-can-reap-the-rewards-of-digital-transformation/) , to learn how modern identity and access management helps you win in the era of Industry 4.0.


### Phase 3: How hackers move laterally from IT to OT across the Purdue Model


A legitimate employee or contractor may pass authentication at the corporate perimeter, but static sign-in verification fails to prevent downstream session exploitation. Attackers deploy infostealer malware through compromised contractor laptops or malicious engineering utilities to extract active session tokens and cookies.


With a valid session in hand, adversaries bypass perimeter checkpoints and maneuver across network zones:


- **Bypassing the IT/OT boundary:** While the classical Purdue Model prescribes strict network segmentation between enterprise IT (Levels 4-5) and industrial control networks (Levels 0–3), modern requirements—such as cloud-connected telemetry, remote monitoring, and edge diagnostics—create necessary digital bridges.
- **Jump server and remote desktop compromise:** Attackers utilize stolen administrative session credentials on dual-homed jump hosts, engineering workstations, or VPN concentrators to pivot directly into MES and supervisory SCADA environments.
- **Concealed dwell time:** Because the attacker operates within an already authenticated session, traditional signature-based security tools fail to detect anomalous administrative navigation until the attacker modifies control logic or triggers ransomware payloads simultaneously.


Without continuous, real-time evaluation of session context—such as device security posture, IP reputation, and impossible travel signals—hijacked sessions can persist undetected across both enterprise and industrial networks.


### Phase 4: How third-party vendor access exposes shop-floor operations


Manufacturing facilities depend on an intricate web of external partners: original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), systems integrators, HVAC specialists, field robotics engineers, and specialized logistics contractors. Many of these third parties require ongoing remote access to calibrate machinery and troubleshoot hardware.


This widespread reliance on external ecosystems introduces deep identity vulnerabilities:


- **Unmonitored third-party backdoors:** Vendors frequently install disparate remote access tools (e.g., TeamViewer, unmanaged RDP, custom VPN tunnels) with standing, 24/7 administrative privileges. If attackers compromise a third-party vendor, that breach directly cascades into the manufacturer’s production network.
- **Access drift and forgotten accounts:** Turnaround contractors, seasonal plant laborers, and retired plant engineers frequently retain Active Directory credentials months or years after their projects conclude.
- **Shared shop-floor credentials:** Across 24/7 multi-shift operations, operators often sign in using generic workstation accounts with hardcoded or taped-on passwords, obscuring user attribution and frustrating incident forensics.


When identity governance relies on fragmented spreadsheets and manual audit reviews, dormant access and unmonitored vendor pathways become the most reliable vectors for intrusion.


## How can manufacturers build an identity-first security architecture?


Securing modern industrial operations requires an identity-first architecture that unifies corporate enterprise environments, distributed supplier ecosystems, and mission-critical OT control layers.


Core principle Modern manufacturing implementation Key operational and compliance drivers


**Phishing-resistant MFA across IT and OT** Enforce FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys and device-bound credentials for all corporate users, remote plant engineers, and third-party remote maintenance sessions. Helps eliminate AiTM credential theft and credential stuffing; satisfies **NIST SP 800-82r3** and **CMMC Level 2/3** MFA mandates.


**Non-human and machine identity governance** Inventory all industrial service accounts, IIoT API keys, and autonomous AI agents; enforce automated secret rotation, short-lived tokens, and strict least privilege. Protects industrial control systems (ICS) from automated lateral traversal; helps prevent industrial espionage and telemetry spoofing.


**Continuous session monitoring and automated signal sharing** Continuously evaluate risk signals (device compliance, impossible velocity, behavioral anomalies); revoke sessions instantly upon token theft or policy violation. Helps stop infostealer malware and session hijacking before attackers pivot into plant-floor MES and SCADA networks.


**Converged identity governance and administration and just-in-time privileged access** Automate onboarding and deprovisioning across ERP and HR systems; eliminate standing remote access for OEMs and contractors in favor of time-bound, audited, approved elevation. Mitigates supply chain risk; satisfies **IEC 62443-3-3** and **NIS2** third-party supply chain governance requirements; helps eliminate orphan accounts.


## Connecting the dots: From the top floor to the shop floor


In modern manufacturing, digital identity is no longer an isolated IT administrative task—it is an indispensable pillar of operational resilience, worker safety, and brand protection.


[Closing industrial attack surfaces](https://www.okta.com/industries/manufacturing/) requires eliminating outdated assumptions about perimeter defenses and static logins. Manufacturing leaders can help secure both their enterprise cloud and their physical production lines by establishing:


- Phishing-resistant authentication for critical human access points
- Rigorous lifecycle governance for third-party vendors and contractors
- Disciplined control over machine and AI identities
- Continuous session risk verification
